source.title: ByteFlow: Language Modeling through Adaptive Byte Compression without a Tokenizer
source.authors: Chunyuan Deng; Sanket Lokegaonkar; Colin Lockard; B. Fetahu; Nasser Zalmout; Xian Li

record.file_problem: none; the complete paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures validation bits-per-byte loss across training trajectories and compares downstream scores at two model scales, but does not fit or test the original scaling-law equations.
record.gate_note: Figure 2 reports validation BPB curves for six architecture families at two scales. Table 1 reports six-task average accuracy at two size/training-token settings. The paper does not report power-law fits, small-run predictions of larger runs, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Chunking and efficiency ablations are not rows because they do not measure a claim version's scaling relationship. Table 2 relies on cited Llama results and is not a controlled scaling comparison.
record.test_reason: An architecture paper. Its 'scaling experiments' compare ByteFlow Net with five baselines at two settings: 600M parameters on 50B byte tokens and 1.3B on 500B. These settings change size and data together. The paper fits no power law, makes no extrapolation, runs no compute-allocation sweep and no within-family shape sweep. It uses Hoffmann et al.'s Chinchilla ratio only to set token budgets, and mislabels them (1x and 4x). Its results are its own method's performance against baselines, so it does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that ByteFlow Net beats BPE and byte-level baselines on BPB and downstream tasks, with a 'superior scaling trajectory'. That scaling claim rests on only two settings (600M/50B and 1.3B/500B) that change size and data together, and on training curves. They do not fit or test scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses byte-level models and reports validation BPB trajectories and downstream comparisons, but does not reproduce the original scaling-law fitting procedure or fit parameter, token, and compute exponents.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture family changes the reported scaling trajectory; the two model-size settings also use different training-token amounts (50B versus 500B).

fits_no_version.finding: The authors claim the downstream gap between ByteFlow and BPE Llama widens with scale: +1.74 points at 600M/50B (50.89 vs 49.15) and +3.04 at 1.3B/500B (63.19 vs 60.15). The evidence is two confounded settings, with no fitted exponents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling trajectories (loss or accuracy against scale) differ by tokenisation and architecture family, with tokenizer-free hierarchical models scaling more favourably.

record.code_released: not stated; the authors say release is pending legal review.
record.problems: Only two model sizes are compared, and their training-token amounts differ substantially. No scaling-law exponents, fit diagnostics, extrapolation checks, or compute-optimal allocation analysis are reported. Figure 2 provides curves without numerical loss values. The text contains inconsistent or varying training-scale descriptions across sections.
record.rows_left_out: Excluded chunking-strategy loss and accuracy results in Table 3, efficiency comparisons in Table 4, and Canon/compression-ratio ablations in Table 6 because they do not measure the tested scaling or downstream-predictability relationships. Table 2 comparisons use cited Llama baselines and do not provide a controlled scale sweep.

untested.parts: No power-law fit; only two size/data settings, under one order of magnitude in parameters.
No compute-optimal allocation; the Chinchilla ratio is only used to set budgets.
No within-family depth or width sweep at fixed parameters.
No predictive relation between downstream scores and scale or loss is fitted.
No analysis of fitting choices or curve bending.

record.verdict_notes: Reader's labels (V1 supports, V4 limits_scope, V6 supports) removed: two confounded points and training curves cannot test these versions. Other problems: (1) The Chinchilla-ratio labels are wrong. About 20 tokens per parameter gives roughly 12B for 600M and 26B for 1.3B, so 50B and 500B are not 1x and 4x. (2) The paper uses 'tokens' and 'bytes' interchangeably. (3) The 1.3B panel of Figure 2 only reaches about 350B bytes, although Table 1 says 500B. (4) Appendix descriptions of the baselines are inconsistent: SpaceByte is called entropy-driven, and BFlowNet is described with regex chunking. (5) Data and step counts differ between ByteFlow (1.95M steps) and the baselines (950K steps). Table 2 uses cited Llama 3 numbers.

versions.untested_parts: The reported loss trajectories concern training-data scaling; the paper does not fit power laws, test parameter- or compute-scaling, or establish the claim over several orders of magnitude.
No predictions fitted on small runs are compared with larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token growth rates are reported.
The architecture families differ in more than depth and width, and the paper does not isolate those factors or report exact plotted loss values.
The experiments concern text pretraining; other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, and transfer are not tested.
Downstream scores are compared at two scales, but the paper does not fit a predictive relationship to scale or pretraining loss; training-token amounts also differ.
The paper does not examine how exponents or compute-optimal splits depend on fitting choices, nor test whether curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: ByteFlow Net
rows.operation_detail: Validation BPB over the training trajectory
rows.note: The text says ByteFlow Net improves steadily and overtakes the LLaMA baseline around the 25B token mark. No fitted power law or numerical curve values are given.
rows.check: Training-trajectory BPB from a single run, given only as a figure. A loss falling over training steps cannot show power-law form across parameters, tokens or compute. The row mainly compares the study's own method with baselines (it overtakes Llama near 25B bytes).

rows.subject: ByteFlow Net

rows.note: The text describes ByteFlow Net as having the most favorable scaling trajectory among the tested architectures. No fitted power law or numerical curve values are given.
rows.check: Same as F2-L600: a figure-only training curve from one run, used to compare the authors' architecture with baselines. It cannot show power-law loss or shape-insensitivity.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: ByteFlow Net validation BPB trajectories at 600M and 1.3B
reader_labels.reason: The paper describes improving validation loss over training and a favorable trajectory at both scales, but does not test power-law shape; rows F2-L600 and F2-L1300.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The authors report that ByteFlow Net overtakes LLaMA in the 600M trajectory and has the most favorable trajectory at 1.3B, indicating architecture-family differences, but the figure supplies no exact losses and does not isolate depth or width; rows F2-L600, F2-L1300, F2-L600-Llama, F2-L1300-Llama.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Six-task averages across the two reported model-size/token settings
reader_labels.reason: Average downstream accuracy is higher at the 1.3B/500B-token setting than at 600M/50B tokens for each listed model family; the comparison is only across these two settings and is confounded by training-token amount; rows T1-600-Llama, T1-1300-Llama, T1-600-LlamaByte, T1-1300-LlamaByte, T1-600-MambaByte, T1-1300-MambaByte, T1-600-SpaceByte, T1-1300-SpaceByte, T1-600-AUNet, T1-1300-AUNet, T1-600-ByteFlow, T1-1300-ByteFlow.
